source: Ash and Hu (2026) WIP Chat-Debugging: LLM as a hardware debugging assistant
finding: Single-student case study of GPT-4o helping debug physical circuits (Pi Pico, I2C mux, LED/battery). Themes: accurate hardware info, handles terse natural-language prompts, higher self-reported confidence.
numbers: N=1 fourth-year EE student, 3 chat logs (Conversation 3 = 7 prompts over 30 minutes), one interview, two coders. No quantitative outcome.
limits: Self-reported confidence rose; no measure of whether confidence matched correctness. Single participant, no control, no bug-fix rate or time data. Authors say a controlled multi-student study is in progress.
agent_relevance: The headline 'boosts confidence' is the G10 risk, not a win: confidence gain without a calibration check. Agent should log hypotheses with evidence and not treat user comfort as success.
quote: LLM outputs cannot be trusted without real-world analysis.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) WIP Chat-Debugging (challenges)
finding: Hardware debugging took many prompts; software bugs usually fixed in one prompt. The LLM drifted from the real circuit over long chats and misread a pin question (GP15 as power input) until the student corrected it.
numbers: Software: usually 1 prompt. Hardware: multiple root causes offered, student ran test plans and fed back results. Context was given in small pieces to avoid overload.
limits: Anecdotal, one student. Drift attributed to long context; not measured.
agent_relevance: Supports a persistent circuit-state record restated each turn, and user-led correction. Agent should keep a ground-truth setup summary and re-assert it.
quote: it does start to forget things or modify things that you had already told it.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) WIP Chat-Debugging (protocol and background)
finding: Proposes mapping LLM help onto Katz and Anderson's four steps (understand, test, locate, fix); LLM drafts test plans and lists multiple root causes; human runs tests. Cites that experts and novices both struggle to generate several hypotheses.
numbers: Cites over 40% of electronics engineers' time spent troubleshooting (industry trade articles, not studies).
limits: Protocol is proposed, not tested. Background cites trade press for the 40% figure.
agent_relevance: Matches our loop: hypothesis list, discriminating test, update. The human is the measurement arm, so the agent must request specific measurements, not assume results.

source: Hu, Chen, Lv, Zhang, Xia (2026) When LLMs Over-Answer: HDL question answering
finding: On 363 stratified Stack Overflow HDL questions (from 6,246), 19 hardware engineers rated LLM vs accepted human answers. LLMs over-answer: multiple alternatives and padding.
numbers: Redundant core answer 65.7% LLM vs 4.4% human. Verbose 69.1% vs 5.8%. Full coverage of accepted answer 50.7%, partial 41.3%, missing 7.7%. Readability preferred: LLM 58.3%, human 35.1%, tie 6.6%.
limits: Engineers had only 1-3 years experience. Accepted answers are a noisy gold standard. Authors say the coverage gap is not a direct correctness failure.
agent_relevance: Fluent, readable, hedged lists look authoritative. Agent should converge to a ranked single next test rather than a dump of alternatives.

source: Hu et al. (2026) When LLMs Over-Answer (task breakdown)
finding: Issue rate varies by category. Debugging questions show elevated redundancy and verbosity in the figure table; generation worst on redundancy.
numbers: Figure 3 issue rates per category, e.g. Debugging 39/52/68/67 across the four columns (Conceptual 36/41/59/68; Generation 44/60/76/78; Optimization 28/48/70/74).
limits: Read from a text-extracted figure table; column labels not fully verified.
agent_relevance: Debugging answers are not exempt from over-answering; add a conciseness gate.

source: Hu et al. (2026) When LLMs Over-Answer (mitigation)
finding: A multi-agent debate plus category-specific compression framework cuts redundancy and padding on four LLMs.
numbers: Core-answer quality 3.71 to 4.67 (+0.96) on a 5-point scale; non-core quality 3.72 to 4.23 (+0.51); core answers down 37% (4.00 to 2.51); non-core length down 31% (1043 to 717).
limits: Scored by LLM-as-judge plus structural counts, not by engineers resolving real bugs. Consistency with accepted answer preserved or slightly improved.
agent_relevance: An internal prune-the-alternatives debate step is cheap and measurable; gains came from structure, not a single model.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench: LLM agents on real hardware bug repair
finding: 417 real bug-fix tasks from six open-source hardware repos (Verilog/SystemVerilog and Chisel). Best agent resolves 70.7%; below 65% on SoC-scale projects.
numbers: Overall best 70.7%. Easier tier (CVA6, Ibex, Caliptra): best above 90%; XiangShan and OpenTitan 20-30 points lower; Rocket Chip best 62.5% vs OpenTitan 64.1% despite 30x less code. Weakest model on easy tier still above 50%.
limits: Task is repair from a bug report in a containerized repo with native simulation, not physical-bench debugging. Hard tier driven by bug type and scope, not repo size.
agent_relevance: Hardware repair is feasible for agents when a simulator gives execution feedback; accuracy depends on bug type, so agent confidence should be conditioned on bug class.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench failure modes
finding: Main failure is fault localization: agents edit the file where the symptom appears, not the file that owns the bug. Second: patches that compile but break the hardware contract (state-machine transitions, valid-ready handshakes).
numbers: Examples: Ibex illegal-instruction bug fixed in controller instead of fetch stage; XiangShan TLB width bug rewritten in TLB module while the true fix was a package-level definition. Agents relying on keyword match are most prone.
limits: Qualitative analysis of failed cases; frequency of each mode only described as a significant fraction.
agent_relevance: Direct match for symptom-versus-cause confusion. Agent needs an explicit step to trace upstream of where the symptom shows (backward reasoning) before editing.

source: Pinckney et al. (2025) CVDP: Comprehensive Verilog Design Problems
finding: 783 engineer-written problems in 13 categories including debugging. Best model gets no more than 34% pass@1 on generation; debug category is higher than most others.
numbers: Highest aggregate non-agentic pass@1 33.56% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet), GPT-4.1 28.91%, Llama 405B 22.79%, Llama 70B 17.53%. Debug/bug-fix category (cid16) Claude 3.7 Sonnet 53.0% and 51.0% (two prompt variants), thinking mode 31% and 45%, GPT-4.1 32% and 26%. n=5 samples per problem.
limits: Extended thinking variant scored lower than plain on debugging. Only 36 debug problems in the table row, so wide uncertainty.
agent_relevance: More reasoning tokens did not help debugging here; do not assume longer chains are safer.

source: Yu et al. (2026) ChipBench: debugging, generation and reference models
finding: On 89 systematic debugging cases, debugging beats generation for the same module. Giving waveforms often does not help.
numbers: Claude-opus 47.45% debugging vs 30.74% generation. One-shot debugging with a .vcd waveform beat zero-shot on 8 models and was worse on 13. Reference-model generation below 50% pass.
limits: Waveform given as raw .vcd text in the prompt; a tool-based reader might do better (authors suggest this).
agent_relevance: Raw measurement dumps can hurt. Agent should summarise measurements into structured observations rather than paste raw traces.

source: Wang et al. (2026) VeriPilot: LLM Verilog debugging with golden reference models
finding: Framework aligns design signals to a golden model and traces signals through control-data-flow graphs. Reports GPT-4o repair success 54.3% to 77.1% in the body; abstract line says 85.71%.
numbers: 54.3% to 77.1% on the benchmark in the body; 54.3% to 85.71% in the abstract line I saw.
limits: Read abstract and introduction only; two different end figures appear and the settings were not reconciled. Needs a golden reference model, which real bench debugging often lacks.
agent_relevance: Structured tracing against an external reference beats free-form guessing: supports tool-grounded checks over self-judgment.

source: Meng et al. (2026) VeriBugBench: constructing Verilog RTL debugging benchmarks
finding: Benchmark-construction framework: 19 inverse mutation operators from real bug-fix histories, LLM testbench enhancement, execution-based retention.
numbers: Mutation library of 19 executable inverse repair patterns. No LLM debugging success rates reported.
limits: Abstract-level read only. Mutation-made bugs may not match organic faults.
agent_relevance: Benchmark bugs are synthetic, so scores may not transfer to organic hardware faults; treat benchmark gains cautiously.

source: Rahman, Hasan, Ahmed, Sultana (2026) Evaluating LLMs on real-world consumer device repair questions
finding: 991 Reddit repair questions (phone, computer, data recovery) with technician reference answers; six LLMs scored on correctness, completeness, practicality (1-5) and safety (binary) by an LLM judge, in English and Bangla.
numbers: GPT-5.4 best overall, up to 0.84 on English data recovery. Phone repair hardest and most safety-sensitive; errors in board-level diagnosis, repair prioritisation, safe recovery. Bangla below English across models.
limits: LLM-as-judge scoring; Reddit questions are incomplete and noisy. Per-model numbers are in figures I did not read.
agent_relevance: Physical repair advice is least reliable where hardware risk is highest. Agent should flag irreversible or unsafe steps and ask before them.

source: Sun, Li, Wang, Goette (2025) Large Language Models are overconfident and amplify human bias
finding: Five LLMs on algorithmically built reasoning problems with known answers: all overconfident, overestimating correctness probability by 20-60%.
numbers: Humans 66% accurate and 70% confident (bias about 4%, Prolific). Humans at 100% sure were only 81% accurate. A 10% drop in LLM confidence goes with about 25% drop in accuracy for GPT-4o and o1 (about 13% for Llama 3.1).
limits: Yes/No reasoning puzzles, not hardware. Human sample is one online benchmark.
agent_relevance: Confidence reports from the model are inflated most when it is least sure; use external checks, not self-stated confidence (G10).

source: Sun et al. (2025) overconfident LLMs: human-with-LLM experiment
finding: Showing people the LLM answer raised accuracy but raised confidence more, so human overconfidence grew.
numbers: Accuracy up 5.6 to 7.0 points. Bias up 4.2 points (answer only) and 7.6 points (answer plus LLM confidence), vs baseline bias about 4%. Low-baseline-confidence users: accuracy +8.6 and +11.9, bias +7.0 and +14.1. High-confidence users did not move.
limits: Generic reasoning questions, short exposure, online participants.
agent_relevance: LLM help can make a user surer than warranted. Direct evidence that the Chat-Debugging confidence gain is double-edged.

source: Ghosh and Panday (2026) Dunning-Kruger effect in LLMs
finding: Four models, four benchmarks, 24,000 trials: worse models are more overconfident.
numbers: Kimi K2 accuracy 23.3%, mean confidence 95.7%, ECE 0.726. Claude Haiku 4.5 accuracy 75.4%, confidence 86.0%, ECE 0.122. Gemini 2.5 Pro 80.9% accuracy, 99.5% confidence, ECE 0.185; Gemini 2.5 Flash 70.9%, 97.9%, ECE 0.272. Confidence-correctness correlation weak (best r=0.175; Gemini 2.5 Pro not significant, p=0.406).
limits: Four models only; verbal confidence elicited once; 10-bin ECE; Haiku underconfident on HellaSwag (74.0% conf vs 82.9% acc). Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Model-level calibration varies a lot; do not assume stated confidence is informative, and test the agent for calibration.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Benchmark of black-box confidence elicitation across five LLMs and five dataset types. Verbalized confidence is overconfident; consistency over samples and human-inspired prompts help.
numbers: GPT-4 near-optimal ECE 0.064 on GSM8K (93.6% accuracy); GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. White-box vs black-box AUROC gap narrow (0.522 to 0.605 in their text). Professional-knowledge tasks remain hard.
limits: No method best everywhere; failure prediction near chance (AUROC 0.5) on hard items for weaker models.
agent_relevance: Use sampling-consistency plus ranked alternatives for confidence, not a single verbal number.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Without external feedback, asking the model to review and fix its own answer does not help and often hurts.
numbers: On GSM8K GPT-3.5 kept its original answer 74.7% of the time; among changes, more correct answers became wrong than wrong became correct.
limits: Reasoning benchmarks, GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era; oracle-feedback gains in earlier papers were an artifact of using labels.
agent_relevance: In hardware, real measurements are the external feedback. Agent should revise after a measurement, not after self-critique (G10).

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know
finding: People overestimate LLM accuracy when given default explanations (calibration gap). Longer explanations raise confidence without raising accuracy. Matching explanation wording to model confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: 301 participants across Experiments 1 and 2 (284 retained). Model confidence AUC 0.751 (GPT-3.5), 0.746 (PaLM2), 0.781 (GPT-4o short answer); human AUC with default explanations only 0.589, 0.602, 0.592. Mean human AUC 0.54 (long) and 0.57 (short) in Experiment 2.
limits: General knowledge questions, no domain experts. Fictitious assistant in a lab.
agent_relevance: Long fluent explanations inflate trust. Keep explanations short and state uncertainty in line with real confidence.

source: Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu et al. (2024) I'm not sure, but... uncertainty expression and reliance (FAccT)
finding: Pre-registered N=404 experiment: first-person uncertainty phrases lower agreement with the AI and raise accuracy; reduces but does not remove overreliance.
numbers: Agreement with system: control 80.9% vs 74.8%, 77.6% and 58.4% in other conditions. Accuracy with AI 63.9% vs 74.2% without AI (the AI itself only 50.0% accurate; medical questions).
limits: Fictional search engine, medical questions, deliberately low-accuracy AI. Table values only partly aligned in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Wording of uncertainty matters; first-person hedges are a cheap way to reduce misplaced trust.

source: Becker, Rush, Barnes, Rein (METR) (2025) Impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developers
finding: RCT of 16 experienced developers on 246 real tasks: AI allowed made them 19% slower, while they forecast 24% faster and afterwards believed 20% faster.
numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks (mean about 2 hours), 143 hours of screen video labelled. Forecast -24% time; post-hoc belief -20%; measured +19%. Experts predicted 39% (economics) and 38% (ML) shorter.
limits: Small N, early-2025 tools, expert developers on familiar large repos; authors say artifacts cannot be fully excluded. Not hardware.
agent_relevance: Perceived and real benefit can diverge by about 40 points. Self-reported confidence gains in Chat-Debugging should not be read as skill gains.

source: Perry, Srivastava, Kumar, Boneh (2023) Do users write more insecure code with AI assistants?
finding: 47 participants, five security tasks: assistant users wrote less secure code and rated it more secure.
numbers: Correct solutions 67% (AI) vs 79% (control). Secure 36% (AI) vs 50% (control) in one task. Many accepted the AI solution without extra verification; 87% of secure responses needed significant edits to the AI output.
limits: Task-specific; Codex-era assistant. Software, not hardware.
agent_relevance: Overreliance without verification is the mechanism; agent should demand a verification step before declaring a fix.

source: O'Brien, Alves, Baltes, Liebel, Lungu, Kalinowski (2026) User misconceptions of LLM-based conversational programming assistants
finding: Qualitative analysis of WildChat Python conversations finds misplaced expectations about web access, code execution and non-text output, and misunderstanding of what information is needed for debugging.
numbers: WildChat sample: 6.7% of 1,000 random prompts were coding-related. Notes a user-synthesizer gap propensity for overconfidence in prior studies.
limits: Software chats, qualitative; not hardware. Authors call for clearer capability disclosure.
agent_relevance: Users assume the LLM can see or run the circuit. Agent should state plainly that it cannot observe the hardware and ask for measurements.

source: Synthesis across opened sources (benchmarks vs human studies)
finding: Benchmark gains appear only with execution feedback (HWE-Bench 70.7%, VeriPilot 54.3% to 77.1%), while human studies show confidence rising faster than accuracy. No study found measures real bench debugging success with and without an LLM.
numbers: Ash and Hu list the controlled study as future work.
limits: This line is my synthesis, not a source finding. Search coverage was limited: arXiv and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited, three web searches used.
agent_relevance: Evidence gap: the key claim (LLM aids physical hardware debugging) has no controlled outcome data yet. Treat as untested; design the agent to be measurable.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench vs software benchmarks
finding: On SWE-bench Verified the same models cluster between 73% and 81%, but on hardware repair they spread more widely, so hardware separates models that software hides.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified 73-81% vs HWE-Bench best 70.7% with larger gaps between models; best agent precision trade-off noted (one model highest resolve rate but lowest precision 0.619).
limits: Different task sets and scaffolds; comparison is descriptive.
agent_relevance: Software-debugging results do not transfer cleanly to hardware; test the agent on hardware tasks directly.
